Because a damaged battery can “wake back up,” the car may be monitored with a thermal camera and parked away from buildings after extinguishment. Compared with gasoline cars, EVs carry less flammable liquid but pose this longer cooling phase and a higher chance of re‑ignition. Bottom line: fire is still fought with water, but for EVs the emphasis is on deep, patient cooling and careful follow‑up rather than quick knockdown.

Short answer: you can make free neutrons and guide or even briefly trap some of them, but you can’t keep a jar of neutrons on a shelf. Neutrons are born inside atomic nuclei; to “separate” them you use nuclear reactions—splitting heavy atoms in a reactor, knocking them out with high‑energy particles (spallation), or using compact neutron generators. Once free, a neutron is tricky: it has no electric charge, so electric fields can’t hold it, and it slips through most materials. It also isn’t immortal—after about 15 minutes on average it turns into a proton, an electron, and a neutrino. The only way we “store” them is to make them very slow and cold so they bounce off special walls or are held by gentle magnetic and gravitational fields; these “ultracold” neutrons can be bottled for minutes, roughly as long as their natural lifetime. Think of trying to keep fog in a colander, and only when the fog is chilled into lazy snowflakes do they bounce around inside the bowl for a little while.

Even without long-term storage, free neutrons are hugely useful. As beams, they act like X‑rays with a different personality: they see the positions of light atoms and the magnetic arrangement inside materials, so scientists use them to map crystal structures, study magnets, and image objects in industry and archaeology. Their knack for being captured by nuclei lets us make medical and industrial isotopes and perform sensitive chemical analysis. Briefly stored ultracold neutrons are a precision playground: they let physicists measure the neutron’s lifetime, test how gravity acts on matter at tiny scales, and hunt for a tiny built‑in electric “lopsidedness” that could help explain why the universe favors matter over antimatter. If you want a truly long‑term neutron “storage,” you need a cosmic‑scale container—a neutron star—where gravity does what no lab bottle can.

Short answer: usually not “really bad,” but not ideal. If the bottle was never opened, water stays safe for months when kept cool and out of sunlight; it may taste flat but it’s fine to drink. Once you’ve sipped from it, your mouth seeds the bottle with microbes. Leave that opened bottle warm for a couple of days and you’ve made a tiny picnic spot for germs. In a fridge, growth is slower, so an opened bottle is generally fine for a day or two. If it smells or tastes odd, or looks cloudy, pour it out. People with weak immune systems, infants, and the very elderly should be more cautious.

Think of a forgotten bottle in a hot car like a little greenhouse: warm, wet, and sometimes sunny—great for microbes and not great for taste. Practical rules: finish opened water the same day when possible; refrigerate if you’ll keep it, and try to use it within 24–48 hours. If it’s been sitting warm or in the sun for a day or more, dump it. Reusable bottles should be washed daily with soap, including the cap and straw, then air‑dried. Single‑use plastic bottles can be reused occasionally, but cleanliness matters more than the plastic itself; avoid heat to prevent off‑flavors. When in doubt, refresh—clean water is cheap insurance.

Short answer: probably not. If you set 100 penguins down “at the North Pole,” they’d be on drifting sea ice with no land to nest on, surrounded by polar bears and long swims to food. Penguins need stable, ice-free ground or very stable sea ice to lay eggs and raise chicks, and the central Arctic doesn’t provide that. Even if you placed them on nearby Arctic coasts or islands, they would meet new land predators like arctic foxes and polar bears. In Antarctica most penguins breed where no land predators exist, so their slow, ground-based colonies work; in the Arctic, being a flightless, ground-nesting bird is a dangerous lifestyle.

Food and timing would also be a problem. Penguins are tuned to Southern Ocean rhythms—spring blooms of plankton that feed krill and small fish right when chicks need feeding. The Arctic has its own seasonal pulse, but it’s different in timing and species, and there are already “penguin-equivalents” there—puffins, murres, and guillemots—that fill the same fish-eating niche. Those northern birds can fly to escape predators and commute to distant feeding grounds, an advantage penguins don’t have. Add unfamiliar diseases and competitors, and the odds that a small, transplanted group could survive, breed successfully, and grow are very low.

Short answer: it doesn’t. Hydraulic fracturing happens a few kilometers down, cracking tight rock to release oil and gas by pumping water and sand at high pressure. Volcanoes, by contrast, are powered by rising magma stored many kilometers deeper, moving enormous volumes over years to centuries. Picture an ant tapping the hide of an elephant: the tap is real, but it doesn’t steer the elephant. The energy, depth, temperature, and pressures involved in volcanic systems dwarf anything created by fracking.

What fracking can do is trigger small, local earthquakes and slightly change stresses in the shallow crust, and large-scale wastewater disposal (a separate activity) has, in some places, produced moderate earthquakes. Even so, these stress changes are tiny compared with those needed to mobilize magma. Studies have found no credible cases of fracking or wastewater injection triggering a volcanic eruption. The only plausible way humans could nudge an eruption would be by directly disturbing a magma body or dramatically pressurizing the hot hydrothermal system right above it—activities that are avoided by regulation and practice. So while fracking may rattle the local “porcelain,” it doesn’t pull the lever on Earth’s deep “pressure cookers.”

Both. The skin on your soles is born different, and then daily use adds extra armor on top.

Think of your palms and soles as the body’s built‑in work gloves. Even in a newborn, the sole has a naturally thicker outer layer, tighter “weave” of supportive fibers, no hair, lots of sweat glands for grip, and springy fat pads underneath. This design spreads out pressure and resists wear, like a tough rubber sole on a shoe. So compared with your forearm or belly, the underside of your foot starts out thicker and tougher by default.

Walking, running, and rubbing then teach that skin to toughen further. Repeated pressure signals the body to stack more dead skin cells on the surface, forming calluses—your own detachable “sandals.” These thicken most where the load is greatest, can build up or fade depending on use, and usually protect without wiping out feeling. Footwear, terrain, and gait shape where and how much callus forms. Too much, too dry, or uneven callus can crack or hurt, but moderate, well‑hydrated callus is a normal, useful adaptation layered on top of already specialized sole skin.

Because wind is a thin, gentle river of energy, you need a very big “net” to catch enough of it. A turbine’s blades sweep a giant circle, and the amount of wind you can catch is proportional to the area of that circle. Make the blades twice as long and you don’t get twice the energy—you get roughly four times, because the circle’s area explodes as the radius grows. Height matters too: winds a few dozen meters higher are usually faster and steadier, and a small bump in wind speed gives a big jump in power. So long blades and tall towers are like fishing with a wide net from the top of a pier, not a small one at the shoreline.

Big machines are also cheaper per unit of energy. One large turbine needs one foundation, one set of electronics, and one crew to maintain it; ten small ones need ten of everything. Large rotors turn more slowly, which keeps noise down and reduces wear, like using a big, easy-turning bicycle gear to push hard rather than spinning your legs furiously. And because turbines create windy “shadows” behind them, packing lots of small ones close together makes them steal wind from each other. Fewer, larger turbines spaced well apart capture more of the sky’s thin power with less fuss—hence those giant, graceful pinwheels on hilltops and at sea.

Hunger isn’t a straight-line “low fuel” alarm; it comes in waves. Overnight, your body expects breakfast at roughly the time you usually eat, so a hunger hormone (ghrelin) rises and your stomach does stronger “housekeeping” contractions that feel like pangs. If you don’t eat, that wave naturally recedes in about 60–90 minutes because these signals pulse on a schedule. Think of it like a tide: it comes in around your usual mealtime and, even without food, it goes back out for a while.

Meanwhile, your body quietly bridges the gap. The liver releases stored sugar to keep your blood glucose steady, stress-and-wakefulness hormones in the morning help mobilize fuel, and fat begins to break down, with by-products that can subtly blunt appetite. Once the brain senses “fuel is available,” it turns down the volume on hunger. Distraction also matters: getting up, showering, or starting work reduces how loud those signals feel. If waiting out a wave leaves you shaky, sweaty, or confused, or if you’re losing weight unintentionally, talk to a clinician to rule out low blood sugar or other issues. Otherwise, what you’re noticing is a normal ebb and flow of the body’s meal-timing system.
